# 14. Working with an AI agent (MCP)

Every project has an MCP (Model Context Protocol) server (`<game>_mcp` from the checkout build, or
the stock `mce_mcp --module <lib<game>.so>`, `mce mcp` with the SDK) that gives an AI agent
the same scene-editing commands a person has in the editor, plus cook and headless verification.
Three games in the repository were authored entirely this way (Kindle's level, Prism Break and
Undertow), and a fourth (Lamplighter) by an agent that had never seen the engine source. This
chapter is the workflow that worked and the pitfalls it found.

## 14.1 Starting the server

```sh
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --scene scenes/main.mcscene
build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/my_game_mcp --project projects/MyGame --allow-cheats
build/<preset>/src/editor/mcp/mce_mcp --module build/<preset>/projects/MyGame/libmy_game.so --project projects/MyGame
mce mcp MyGame                                      # the SDK: the line above with its own paths
```

# Kindle

The UC-D proof game (ROADMAP M9, `docs/milestones/M9-ucd.md`): one small 2D level made with the
MCE project template and the project editor's MCP server. It reuses Ember Step's mechanics (the
platformer controller, coins, spikes, the goal flag, crumbling blocks, a moving platform) as authored
components, and adds one mechanic: **colour switches**. Touching a switch swaps which block colour
is solid. Red starts solid; the red wall needs the first switch, the blue bridge over the pit needs

# A level that a bot can finish

You want a new level that is provably finishable, and a test that fails the day it stops being so.

1. **Reuse a level's skeleton.** `scene_open` an existing level, `scene_list_entities` to see its
   camera, player, ground and goal, then `scene_save {"path": "scenes/level2.mcscene"}`: a copy with
   its own path. (A fresh `scene_new` gets a new GUID; add it to the game's level list.)
2. **Lay it out.** `entity_duplicate` a platform and `component_set` its
   `LocalTransform.position` for each new one; name them (`Ledge 1`, `Ledge 2`). Keep the player and
   the goal named `Player` and `Goal`. `scene_save`.
3. **Look.** `render_sheet {"ticks": [1, 60, 180]}` shows the level as the player draws it.
4. **Play it.** For a side view:

   ```json
   { "bot": { "kind": "walk_to", "actor": "Player", "target": "Goal", "plane": "x" }, "ticks": 1800 }
   ```

   `playtest` returns the feel report. `finished: true` and a `time_to_finish_s` you expect mean
   the level works. `stuck_spots` say where the bot could not get on (a gap too wide, a wall too
   high): `render_frame` with `camera: {"center": [x, y], "zoom": 1}` at the spot's position shows
   it. Move a ledge and play again.
5. **Keep it.** Save the same arguments as `tests/level2.mctest`, with what must stay true:

   ```json
   {
     "name": "level 2 can be finished",
     "scene": "scenes/level2.mcscene",
     "bot": { "kind": "walk_to", "actor": "Player", "target": "Goal", "plane": "x" },
   [... 511 characters cut]

# Screens that stay right

You want to know when a change breaks how a screen looks, without a person looking.

1. **Get it right once.** `render_frame {"tick": 30}` (and with `input` to reach a moment, e.g.
   `"1-90 Move=1,0"`) until the screen looks as intended. A phone layout:
   `"safe_area": {"top": 48, "bottom": 34}`.
2. **Bless it.** `image_diff {"golden": "goldens/title.png", "render": {"tick": 30}}`: with no golden
   yet, the frame becomes the golden. Do the same for each level's first frame.
3. **Check after every change.** The same call returns `score` (0 is identical), `changed_fraction`
   and `pass` (`score <= max_score`, default 0.01), with a heat map image of what moved. A failing
   score on a screen you did not mean to change is a regression; on one you did, look at the frame
   and pass `update: true` to bless it again.
4. **Several moments at once.** `render_sheet {"ticks": [1, 60, 120, 240], "cameras": [{}, {"center": [12, 3], "zoom": 0.5}]}`
   gives one image to review.

Frames come from the real player (offscreen software rendering without a display), so the same
arguments give the same pixels on the same machine. Keep goldens in the project (they are PNG files
under any folder you choose) and commit them with the scenes.

# 11. Input

Gameplay never sees keys, buttons or SDL events. Each fixed tick the engine folds every device
event into one immutable snapshot, `input::InputState`, and your systems read that. The snapshot
is part of the determinism contract: it can be recorded and replayed, and the same snapshot
sequence gives the same game.

## 11.1 Reading input

```cpp
void player(Frame& f) {
    const input::InputState& in = f.resource<input::InputState>();
    const f32 mx = in.move.x;                 // -1..1, WASD / arrows / left stick / d-pad
    if (in.jump_pressed) { ... }              // edge: this tick only
    if (in.jump_held) { ... }                 // level
    if (in.fire_pressed) { ... }
    if (in.pause_pressed) { ... }
    const bool dash = in.has_action(MCE_SID("Dash")) ? in.pressed(MCE_SID("Dash")) : in.fire_pressed;
}
```

| Member | Action | Default bindings |
|---|---|---|
| `move` (vec2) | Move | W A S D, arrows, left stick, d-pad |
| `look` (vec2) | Look | mouse delta, right stick |
| `jump_pressed` / `jump_held` / `jump_released` | Jump | Space, gamepad South (A) |
| `fire_pressed` | Fire | J, left mouse, gamepad West (X) |
| `pause_pressed` | Pause | Escape, Start |
| `confirm_pressed`, `cancel_pressed` | Confirm, Cancel (UI map) | Enter or Space, Escape; South, East |
| `text()` | typed text this tick (UTF-8) | |
| `mouse_pos_px()`, `mouse_wheel()` | pointer state at the tick's end | |

contents.text:
# 7. 2D games

The 2D path is a set of scene-authored components (the "kit") that the player draws for you:
sprites, text, a camera, parallax layers, 2D lights, post effects, tilemap layers and particle
emitters. Your game code changes their fields; nothing in your module draws.

Units are metres with +Y up. An entity's `LocalTransform` places the sprite's pivot, its rotation
about Z turns the quad, and its scale multiplies `size`.

## 7.1 Sprites

| Field | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `texture` | the image; a null reference draws a solid quad in `tint` |
| `normal_map` | tangent-space normal map for 2D lighting (import with `srgb: false`) |
| `tint` | colour multiplier in **linear** RGB (see below); `tint.a` fades the sprite |
| `size` | world size in metres; the texture is stretched to it |
| `pivot` | normalized, `[0.5, 0.5]` centre, `[0, 0]` bottom-left |
| `layer`, `order` | stacking: `layer` first (−100..100), then `order` within the layer, then ECS order |
| `flip_x`, `flip_y` | mirror |
| `region` | the part of the texture shown, `[u0, v0, u1, v1]` from 0 to 1 with `v0` the top edge; `[0, 0, 1, 1]` (the default) is the whole texture |

`region` picks a frame out of an atlas by hand; an `AnimatedSprite` (7.3) writes it for you.
Missing or broken textures draw as a magenta checker rather than nothing.

Sprites are point-sampled by default, which keeps pixel art crisp. For smooth, painted or

# 15. Shipping

One command builds, cooks, packages and zips a game:

```sh
python3 scripts/ship.py --project projects/MyGame
python3 scripts/ship.py --project projects/MyGame --version 1.0.0 --preset linux-gcc-release
python3 scripts/ship.py --project projects/MyGame --smoke --smoke-headless   # run it once after packaging
```

Output: `dist/<Name>-<version>-<os>.zip` and, beside it, `<Name>-<version>-<os>-symbols.zip`, where
`<os>` is `linux-x64`, `win64` or `macos`.

| Option | Meaning |
|---|---|
| `--preset` | the CMake preset to build (default: the platform's release preset) |
| `--version` | default `<engine version>+<short commit>` |
| `--out` | output directory (default `dist/`) |
| `--no-build` | package what is already built |
| `--keep-symbols` | do not strip the binaries (Linux, macOS) |
| `--smoke`, `--smoke-headless` | run the packaged game once (headless needs no display) |

The samples ship the same way: `python3 scripts/ship.py platformer` (Ember Step) or `diorama`.

## 15.1 What is in the zip

One folder, double-click the executable (on macOS the folder holds `<Name>.app` and `README.txt`;
see section 15.4):

| File | What |
|---|---|
| `<Name>` (`.exe` on Windows, with icon and version resource) | the host |
| `lib<game>.so` | the game module, `.so` on macOS too (not on Windows, where it is linked in) |
| `libmce_engine.so` | the engine (`libmce_engine.dylib` on macOS) |
| `assets.mce` | the cooked pack, CRC-checked once at mount |
